evidence.text: I think I'm out. I struggled with this one. I really wanted to say yes. I think the product's great. I just - we've done a couple of things in food and it just - it just ends up being hard relative - I mean, everything's hard. The challenges in food, I feel like in many cases there's less under your control. With the road to distribution than there are in some other businesses that we work on where the distribution challenges are hard but they're largely like under your control. That being said, I think you guys are going to be successful. I think the product is great. This one was tough. I was hanging around for a while to see if I could get over the hump -

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: My name is Paul Lehmann, the taller cofounder of Awesome Sauce.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: And I'm Carl, the shorter cofounder of Awesome Sauce, the world's first sustainable sauce company. We're on a mission to change the way sauces are made, distributed and consumed. We're coming after Heinz.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: So let me take you back to the winter of 2020. I was the athletic director at West Town School, and I had a passion for barbeque, spice rubs and sauces and I was convinced, and still am convinced that my sauces are better than your sauces, and I was ready to take that to market. So one day, one of my pain in the ass coaches over here, overhears me talking about my new sauce business, and Carl being Carl, he wanted in. And we knew right then and there that we were not going to join the same old sauce game. We were going to disrupt a 130 billion dollar industry. But how? So we quickly got to the question - can you take the water out of sauce? And the answer is powder. Our sauces come to you as a powder that you mix with water to make all of the delicious sauces that you know and love. And that's how AWSM Sauce was born.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: So in the summer of 2021, we incorporated. By November, we were accepted to Techstars, which got us into the Minnesota Twins Stadium. We took the next year to test ecomm, retail, restaurants, really understanding our product feedback and where product market fit was. And what we landed on was: food service. Where for decades the same boring sauces have been given away for free out of the same gross dispensers and there's little to no value given to the concessionaire. But we changed that. With our sauce, we decrease plastic packaging, we have an innovative and customizable solution that, at scale, matches the cost of leading brands. So we're here raising $3 million to change the sauce game forever. Who wants to get lost in the sauce ?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: I'm gonna put some fries on the plate so...

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Oh please, that's my vice, pop tarts and fries. Oh, I love fries!

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Same.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: So as you see this, you have ketchup, you have barbeque at the top, and then you have an old Bay style hot sauce.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Oh my gosh.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: It’s called our Chesapeake fire.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: The Chesapeake one's good.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I really like the sauces.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: Thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: Which was your favorite?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Actually, I - maybe the spicy one.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: The Chesapeake one. Chesapeake fire.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: So we got two votes for Fire. That's where I’m living.

turns.text: I'm a Sweet Baby Ray’s guy, and that barbeque sauce right there, I would take that any day.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I would too. It's way better!

turns.speaker: Neal
turns.text: That's delicious. You got me.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: Thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: What's the sugar content of these? Does the sugar content decrease because of this?

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: No. The nutritional facts are about one to one on traditional sauce.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay, good to know

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: It was our priority to match sauces that the consumer was familiar with.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: And then sort of work backwards to a lower sugar, more healthy organic - and trying to think about how can we now take a product that people have belief in and we've got consumer trust to then work back.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Sure.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So tell us, just a little bit more about the product. How do you reduce the pack - the plastic? Like how are you delivering the product?

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: Yeah, so good question. So our packets are a tenth of the weight. So it's a 90% reduction of plastic.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: And then our format decreases the weight, so it's decreasing 66% of scope 3 emissions, so greenhouse gases associated to, to traveling super heavy liquids.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: You're talking about food service distribution, but your sauce requires a little more work for the food service employees, right? They've got to mix it and - tell us about that.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: So what we want to do is we want to develop a machine that has a touch screen that allows somebody to go up to it and they say, I want ketchup, they not only are offered just ketchup, but they have spicy ketchup, jalapeno ketchup, Jillian ketchup, anybody's ketchup, and then it's dispensed. That's where the customization and the innovation comes in.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Then that wouldn't require anymore work from the employees -

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: Exactly.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: - because the machine is doing the work.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: And our model would be to actually lease that machine to the either the university or stadium and then have a service contract where we would add the powders.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Is your differentiation then, is your real focus on the sustainability to food service or are you selling convenience or taste? Like what's - what's the pitch to them?

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: So the highest level is we are selling sustainability. That is why we exist as a company. However, with this product, taste has to be there. And so our one and one is taste and sustainability. And so when we go into like the university and stadium model with food service, our three value propositions are ESG, so we're reducing emissions and we're reducing packaging; innovative experience, and then at the bottom end is cost. So because of the relationship, there are national contracts, and so our goal and with our format, we're able to hit costs really early. And so our value props are ESG, innovative experience and cost.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: It would seem to me, that their priorities would be flipped, whereas cost would be number one over - I mean, I'm sure more and more of them are ESG-focused now. But I would still imagine that cost is number one.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: And I think the interesting piece to note there is we were in the Minnesota Twins Stadium, so we did this pilot, in 10 minutes we sold a Philadelphia-based team and he said that he would pay more because of the ESG. So a lot of these stadiums, because of their stakeholder agreements, have to meet certain requirements and waste is a big one. And so for us, the waste management, and for them, scope 3, which is the emissions associated to the products that they're moving, the transportation, that's their number one focus. So to be clear, part of these, in the initial phase for us is to come in as a partner to the team. However, because they have a contract with the concessionaire, as we come in at cost parity, then now we have a relationship with a Delaware North or an OVG, and if we prove that to be really beneficial, now we partner just with OVG who's in 40 of the 50 largest stadiums.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: You have the Minnesota Twins, is that - or you you just have the stadium? The whole stadium?

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: We did a pilot with the Minnesota Twins for the month of April. And…

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: And how'd that go?

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: Fantastic.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: They asked us to stay in the stadium for the year.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: Which we were like -

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: We're not ready. I mean, we just -

turns.speaker: Elizabeth

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: Right. And we didn't have dispensers ready, I mean, it was - it's just the two of us at this point in time.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: So talk about that. What does it take to get ready for their stadium? Like what do you need? Minnesota Twins.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: How many dispensers?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth

turns.speaker: Jillian

turns.text: We got a lot of questions coming. I'm taking them. I'm fielding them. All right. So the Minnesota Twins compared to an MLS team that we're gonna work with, they have let's say 40 dispensing stations. Where we were with the Twins is we removed just ketchup. And we put in ketchup, BBQ and fire. So these three. And what was consumed was all three equally. So we proved that consumers do want the optionality of multiple flavors.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I just want to understand, going back to this original question of how can you serve this first contract. Like, what does the rough ballpark amount of cash that you need to be able to fulfill it?

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: Our costs right now - what was it for our first run? 15 grand?

turns.text: It was about 15 grand to service the ballpark.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: a week?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: And that covered the whole season?

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: No. That covers - we'd have to figure - we don't have like what that would have yielded in sauce.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: It would have been about three -

turns.text: I'm getting lost in the sauce here so -

turns.speaker: Phil

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: So it costs 12 cents an ounce to make. That's where we are.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: The sauce costs 12 cents an ounce.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: 12 cents an ounce to make.

turns.speaker: Phil

turns.text: It would depend. Initially, we would come down to 8 cents an ounce to match the cost that they have. So we would eat 4 cents an ounce.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So wait, you're paying 12 cents and you're selling it for 8 cents?

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: That's right.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Let me just think about this for a minute.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: So 12 cents an ounce is where we are right now. turns.text: What kind of volume level do you need to be to get to 5 and a-half cents?

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And your thought would be, okay, we get it down to 5 and a-half cents and you're still going to sell it for 8 cents?

turns.speaker: Carl

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Do you think there's appetite for them to pay more?

turns.speaker: Carl

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Because of the ESG?

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: Correct.

turns.speaker: Jillian

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: one it's, I think that's expensive, unreliable -

turns.text: I guess where I'm going with this is I feel like it's often better to sort of do things piecewise to prove out pieces one part at a time, and derisk pieces one part at a time. Whatever it takes, manual, etc. Maybe some existing machine that could do the purpose without anything crazy, that is the next iteration.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: Correct.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: And then from there replace out to the ideal machine. I don't know if that's your plan.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: It took us a while as a group to get there, but that's the plan!

turns.text: Don't those concessionaires, don't they have exclusivity contracts with Heinz and some of the others?

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: Not exclusive.

turns.text: Well, they're only allowed to carry one ketchup, one type of mustard, one type of -

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: Right. However, as we come in as a partner to the team, then we would be a sauce partner like for the Twins.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: Because they don't serve it. We would serve it.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: But you've been live - clearly you must have negotiated -

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: We have not had that experience. And so because they don't sell sauces, this isn't something where they're guaranteeing a certain amount of revenue.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Like a water or a -

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: Like a water would say, hey, only sell our product, or a beer would only sell this. We're coming in as a partner to the Twins -

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: That's right. They're not selling it.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: Stadiums spend about $100,000 a year on sauce that they give away for free.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: With little to no value.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: No, no, those are important points.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: Well said, Carl.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I have kind of a different question.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: Please.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: Bring it.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: You don't see a lot of breakthrough sauce brands. The last one I can think of is Sir Kensington’s.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: Stop it.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I'm just curious if you have a sense of like - how are they able to be so successful on a relative basis in a category - this isn't like software or some of the other categories where we see many, many successful companies. I mean, they're not the only one, but that's one that I've been thinking about since listening to your story.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: Yeah, my short answer is there's just a lot of room. Like when you think about the category in general, it's $130 billion industry, 60% of which goes towards food service, 40% of which goes through retail. And both of them are hard in general. Heinz is vertically integrated, so they're kind of stuck on pricing, whereas Sir Kensington or Primal Kitchen can kind of come in and move a little bit based on what they're marketing. It doesn't matter if our sauce ultimately is the sauce flowing through those machines. They can take their brand equity and pump that through the machine, and it can be really exciting for the concessionaire, the university or the team. And so what we did is we pioneered something that our powder to pour technology is completely new.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I have a powdered shampoo company in my portfolio, It's actually very difficult to make powder -

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: And for it to yield this way.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: And to yield this consistency, it's very difficult.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: And so, we are understate - we're trying to be as humble as possible, but it's really hard to do it, and we did it.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Are you the only ones?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Do you have a patent?

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: We are the only ones and we have a process patent on this. So the process patent on this is the amount of water stays consistent, it's a third of a cup for every packet. And the yielded consistency is very different. But when we get into the machine side, nobody else is doing this at all, and so we can IP that, which builds that moat so much stronger. We built the brand now and we can take that in front of food service where the cash burn is so much shorter to get volume moving.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Can we hone in on this point that Charles is making - ketchup in particular, there are two brands. Heinz, Hunts, - Heinz has the, you know, dominates, right. I'm sure there are many people who have made ketchup over the years. Why is it that Heinz is so dominant?

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: They're vertically integrated. So they own -

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: It's just cost?

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: It's just cost. They own the farms. But that also - that also pins them. So for them to change on pricing, they'll start to source in different ways.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: But it also shows that everyone is so cost conscious on their ketchup. So how do you compete with that when you are not vertically integrated yet?

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: I I think there’s two ways to answer that question. The first one is do you really need to compete with ketchup? So when we think about sauce, it's across all. Like ketchup is a billion dollars, but so is mayo, and so is BBQ. And so you have to have ketchup, but I think where you win is soy-based BBQ, or we win on peanut Thai sauce, or we win on hot sauces where hot sauce is so popular.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: So I think what I'm getting at is because you made three sauces here for us, I don't actually know in the eyes of a buyer how they see you competing. Are you a ketchup and then by the way you get two extra sauces? Or are you a hot sauce or a BBQ sauce and here's some ketchup.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: Actually, ketchup's really interesting, because it's the one thing that you have to match. I mean BBQ and hot sauce are the wild west. And you can have a sweet BBQ, or a vinegar BBQ or a thick BBQ or not. And so we can really sort of play around in those areas and it's really interesting for us to match ketchup which we think we've done really well.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I think your ketchup's very good. I like it.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: Thank you. And I guess what we've heard from concessionaires, in fact, they don't want to go sourcing their BBQ from them and the hot sauce from here, and the ketchup from there - they're looking for a one stop shop. And the fact that we can do that and, as we think about two years down the road, bring in the machine to really make this an attractive user experience - and I don't know if we've mentioned this but I think what we see is really our first step is universities and stadiums, and the idea behind that is that as we get eyes on the brand through those avenues, that pulls our D2C in a really meaningful way and is effective in ways that we aren't today.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Tell us a bit about your raise. I think initially you said you were raising 3 million..

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: And do you have terms already? Or where are you in that raise?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Is that pre or post?

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: That would be - we'd like to - pre?

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: Pre? That would be great, but I mean we're not gonna say no to money so if it's a post then...

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: I'd rather drink tequila than not drink tequila, so.

turns.speaker: Neal

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: I appreciate it.

turns.speaker: Neal
turns.text: But I got a little piece through Techstars.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: I appreciate that.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: I appreciate that.

turns.text: We'll get there.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And I do appreciate the big vision that you have.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: And we're trying to be as realistic as possible but it's massive.

turns.speaker: Carl
turns.text: But there's no reason not to go for it and then land where we do. So that's why we're raising -

turns.speaker: Elizabeth

turns.speaker: Jillian
